extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in real analysis / advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Formal statements, definitions, and basic theorems about limits at infinity, monotone functions and their continuity properties, the derivative and its basic rules, and the mean value theorems. Intended to guide learning/proof-writing in undergraduate real analysis/calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite limit (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition 3.5.6: f : S ⊂ ℝ → ℝ 'diverges to infinity as x goes to ∞' means: for every N ∈ ℝ there exists M such that whenever x ∈ S and x ≥ M we have f(x) > N. Notation: lim_{x→∞} f(x) = ∞ (or 'f(x) → ∞ as x → ∞'). Similar definitions for x → −∞ and for cluster points at ±∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous sequential characterizations hold (one can use sequences x_n → ∞). The definition can be adapted to limits being −∞ and to finite cluster points; students are invited to state the analogous definitions and verify sequential equivalences (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of limits (Proposition 3.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → ℝ, g : B → ℝ with f(A) ⊂ B (A,B ⊂ ℝ) and a ∈ A is a cluster point of A, and b is the limit of f(x) as x → a (b may be in ℝ ∪ {−∞,∞}), and if lim_{y→b} g(y) = c (with appropriate hypotheses when b is finite), then lim_{x→a} g(f(x)) = c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposition requires the usual compatibility/continuity hypotheses when the intermediate limit b is in the domain of g. Proof is straightforward and left as exercise; see earlier exercises (3.1.9, 3.1.14) for finite-limit analogues. Use sequential limit lemmas to translate statements about sequences into statements about function limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of monotone (Definition 3.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : S ⊂ ℝ → ℝ is increasing if x < y (with x,y ∈ S) implies f(x) ≤ f(y); strictly increasing if x < y implies f(x) < f(y). Decreasing and strictly decreasing are defined by reversing inequalities. 'Monotone' means either increasing or decreasing. 'Nondecreasing' and 'nonincreasing' terminology may be used to emphasize not-strictness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many results are proved for increasing functions and carry over to decreasing functions by switching inequalities. Monotone includes the strictly monotone and constant cases; some statements exclude constant functions to avoid degenerate technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-sided limits for monotone functions (Proposition 3.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S ⊂ ℝ and c is a cluster point of S and f : S → ℝ is increasing, then the left-hand limit at c exists and equals sup{ f(x) : x ∈ S, x < c }, and the right-hand limit at c exists and equals inf{ f(x) : x ∈ S, x > c }. Analogous statements hold for decreasing functions (with sup/inf swapped) and for limits at ±∞ (limits exist and equal suprema/infima of appropriate sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus monotone functions always have all one-sided limits wherever those one-sided approaches make sense. The proof uses monotonicity to bound difference quotients; students are asked to finish similar cases as exercises. In particular continuity at c occurs iff the two one-sided limits coincide and equal f(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity vs image-interval property for monotone functions (Corollary 3.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I ⊂ ℝ be an interval and f : I → ℝ be monotone and not constant. Then f(I) is an interval if and only if f is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction uses intermediate value theorem: if f is continuous on I then f(I) is an interval. Reverse direction: if f(I) is an interval and f is monotone, must show f is continuous; proof proceeds by contradiction using one-sided limits and finding values missing from f(I). Exercises ask for endpoint cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countability of discontinuities of monotone functions (Corollary 3.6.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I ⊂ ℝ is an interval and f : I → ℝ is monotone, then the set of discontinuities of f is at most countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs an injection from the set of non-endpoint discontinuities into ℚ by choosing a rational between the left and right one-sided limits at each discontinuity. Students are guided through constructing the injection and concluding countability. Examples show the bound is sharp (countably many discontinuities can occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse of strictly monotone function is continuous on its range (Proposition 3.6.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I is an interval and f : I → ℝ is strictly monotone (hence injective), then f^{-1} : f(I) → I is continuous (and monotone) on its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: strict monotonicity implies f^{-1} is monotone and the one-sided limits of f^{-1} equal appropriate extrema, forcing equality; hence continuity. Note f itself need not be continuous (example 3.6.7) but the inverse is continuous on the image (which is an interval when f is continuous and onto). Exercises ask to finish edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of derivative (Definition 4.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I be an interval and f : I → ℝ. f is differentiable at c ∈ I if the limit lim_{x→c} (f(x) − f(c))/(x − c) exists; this limit is denoted f'(c). If f is differentiable at every c ∈ I we write f' : I → ℝ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: derivative is slope of tangent line; difference quotient is the secant slope. Definition allows c to be an endpoint (one-sided limit). Several examples follow (polynomials, root, absolute value) illustrating differentiability and non-differentiability. Exercises guide computation of derivatives for common functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiable implies continuous (Proposition 4.1.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at c ∈ I then f is continuous at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses limit decomposition: f(x) − f(c) = (x − c)·(difference quotient) and difference quotient → f'(c) while (x − c) → 0. Exercises cover converse failure (continuous but not differentiable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of the derivative (Proposition 4.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are differentiable at c and α ∈ ℝ, then (α f)'(c) = α f'(c), and (f + g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by direct algebra on difference quotients and passing to limits. Corollary: derivatives are linear operators; exercises ask to apply linearity to combinations of functions and polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product rule (Proposition 4.1.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are differentiable at c then the product h(x) = f(x) g(x) is differentiable at c and h'(c) = f(c) g'(c) + f'(c) g(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the identity decomposing Δ(fg) as f·Δg + g(c)·Δf (or algebraic rearrangement illustrated by area argument in figure). Exercise 4.1.1 asks students to prove it; this is key for computing derivatives of products and polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient rule (Proposition 4.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are differentiable at c and g(x) ≠ 0 for all x ∈ I (in particular g(c) ≠ 0), then h(x) = f(x)/g(x) is differentiable at c and h'(c) = (g(c) f'(c) − f(c) g'(c)) / (g(c))^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof can be done directly or by combining product rule with derivative of reciprocal (exercise hint). Used to differentiate rational combinations of functions; requires denominator nonzero in a neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain rule (Proposition 4.1.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g : I1 → I2 is differentiable at c ∈ I1 and f : I2 → ℝ is differentiable at d = g(c), then the composition h = f ∘ g is differentiable at c and h'(c) = f'(g(c)) · g'(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof presented via auxiliary functions u and v representing the increment quotients, showing continuity and taking limits; exercise-oriented. Chain rule is essential for changing variables and differentiating nested expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical point test: derivative zero at interior extremum (Lemma 4.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable at c and c is a relative maximum or minimum (interior point), then f'(c) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof inspects difference quotients from left and right, using sign constraints from extremum; sequences approaching from both sides show left-hand limit ≤ 0 ≤ right-hand limit, forcing derivative zero. Use when locating candidates for extrema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's theorem (Theorem 4.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a) = f(b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that f'(c) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric idea: continuous function attaining equal endpoint values must have interior max or min; apply Lemma 4.2.2. Hypotheses are essential: differentiability on the open interval cannot be dropped (counterexamples exist). Exercises illustrate edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean value theorem (Theorem 4.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to Rolle's theorem by subtracting an affine function with same endpoint values. Geometric interpretation: some tangent slope equals the secant slope. Many classical applications (estimates, speed-from-average-speed) and generalizations (Cauchy's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's mean value theorem (Theorem 4.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and φ are continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c ∈ (a,b) such that (f(b) − f(a))·φ'(c) = (φ(b) − φ(a))·f'(c), i.e. f'(c)/φ'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(φ(b) − φ(a)) provided φ'(c) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the mean value theorem to two functions and yields a framework for L'Hôpital's rule and other ratio-type estimates. Proof is left as exercise via Rolle's theorem applied to an appropriate combination of f and φ.
